Apple today accused a new UK proposal targeting App Store fees as amounting to price control, warning it could harm innovation and investment. Details below.

Apple pushes back on App Store regulation in the UK

According to a Reuters report, Apple today formally responded to a consultation from the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), opposing a proposed rule that would allow app developers to link to alternative payment methods.

The CMA could impose the rules after designating Apple and Google as having "strategic market status" in their respective mobile platform markets last year. Under the UK's new digital markets regime, such designations allow regulators to introduce rules targeting individual companies to promote competition and give consumers more choice.

Under the proposal, Apple and Google could still charge a commission on transactions completed through alternative payment methods, but any such fees would have to be considered "fair and reasonable".

Reuters noted that the CMA "expects that the cost of steering fees will be lower than current app store fees and that the savings will be passed on to UK consumers or reinvested in developers' businesses to support innovation".

The CMA rejected Apple's characterisation of the proposal as price control, saying its intent was to establish principles for determining whether steering fees are fair and reasonable, rather than to set fee levels directly.
